meta.regime: The regime has rotated from geopolitics back to the Fed, and it did so on a single print. US July nonfarm payrolls contracted by 23,000 against a consensus of +83,000 to +95,000, and the damage in the revisions was worse than the headline: the prior two months were cut by a combined 146,000, leaving June at just +20,000. The unemployment rate technically improved to 4.1% from 4.2%, but that is a participation artefact - the participation rate fell to 61.4%, the lowest in more than five years, meaning the rate fell because people left the labour force rather than because they found work. Average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y, the softest since May 2021, which removes the wage-inflation channel the July dissenters were leaning on. Rate futures responded immediately: the probability of a September hike dropped to 43.9% from 57% and the probability of a hold rose to 60.4%. Friday's file upgraded the dollar to 0 on the strength of Lisa Cook's Anchorage speech, the cycle-low claims run and the 1.3% unit-labour-cost print; that upgrade is reversed here, and USD returns to -1. The second story is Canada, which printed the exact opposite report at the exact same minute: +75,100 jobs, the largest monthly gain in two years, split almost evenly between full-time (+38,600) and part-time (+36,600), with unemployment falling to 6.4% - a two-year low - and participation up to 65.1%. Layer on WTI at $78.82 after a third consecutive session of gains, with Brent at $84.18, and the loonie now has both a labour leg and a terms-of-trade leg for the first time in weeks. CAD is upgraded from 0 to +1. The oil bid persists because Hormuz has not resolved: Iran and Oman have agreed the coordinates of a safe shipping corridor and Araghchi calls the draft very close, but IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi has said the strait's reopening has its own mechanism, is separate from the Oman talks, and depends on the US fully accepting Iran's conditions. The metals have recoupled now that the Fed is the dominant input rather than the war: gold sits at $4,341.94 and silver has reversed two sessions of losses to $64.24, up 1.08%, with the gold-silver ratio down to 67.68 from 68.32. The euro keeps the top of the board on a September 10 hike that is roughly 70% priced, July HICP at 2.9% with core up to 2.5% and euro-area energy inflation accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5% - the exact channel Lagarde tied the hiking bias to. New Zealand remains the anchor short. The cleanest expressions are the ones long a tightening central bank against a stopped one.

dailyRead: The board has rotated from the war back to the Fed, and Friday's payroll report is the reason. US July nonfarm payrolls contracted by 23,000 against expectations of +83,000 to +95,000, and the revisions did more damage than the headline - the prior two months were cut by a combined 146,000, leaving June at just +20,000 rather than the +57,000 previously carried. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, but that is not a strong print: participation dropped to 61.4%, the lowest in more than five years, so the rate improved because people left the labour force. Average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y, the weakest since May 2021, which cuts the wage channel out from under the three July dissenters. Rate futures moved straight away, with September hike odds falling to 43.9% from 57% and hold probability rising to 60.4%. Friday's file upgraded the dollar to 0 on Lisa Cook's Anchorage remarks and the cycle-low claims run; that call is reversed and USD goes back to -1. That restores the dollar-leg trades that came off on Friday: EUR/USD returns to HIGH, GBP/USD and AUD/USD to MEDIUM, USD/CAD to a MEDIUM short, and DXY back to a MEDIUM short. Canada is the mirror image and the day's biggest upgrade. At the same minute the US shed jobs, Statistics Canada reported +75,100, the largest monthly gain in two years, split almost evenly between full-time (+38,600) and part-time (+36,600), with unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% and participation rising to 65.1%. Average hourly wages rose 2.8% y/y to $37.17, which is soft, and both BoC core measures remain below target - CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% - so there is still no rates leg. But the terms-of-trade leg is now real: WTI has risen for a third consecutive session to $78.82 with Brent at $84.18, because the Hormuz question has not resolved. Iran and Oman have agreed the coordinates of a safe corridor and Araghchi calls the draft very close, but IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi has stated that the strait's reopening has its own mechanism, is separate from the Oman negotiation, and requires the US to fully accept Iran's conditions. CAD is upgraded from 0 to +1, which makes NZD/CAD the cleanest short on the board at a four-point gap and USD/CAD a genuine MEDIUM short into a 1.3961 handle. The euro holds the top at +2 and the case is unchanged and strong: July HICP 2.9% with core up to 2.5%, services inflation 3.3%, euro-area energy inflation accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q, composite PMI 52.0, and a September 10 hike around 70% priced - and the ECB explicitly hung that bias on the energy channel that crude has just reopened. Sterling and the Aussie both sit at +1 as followers into their own events: the UK has Q2 GDP on Thursday and a committee that went 6-3 against a 7-2 consensus, while the RBA decides tomorrow at 04:30Z with all 37 economists in the Reuters poll calling a hold - the Statement on Monetary Policy and Bullock's tone are what matter, not the rate. The yen stays at 0 and that is the tell of the session: the dollar was sold hard on Friday and USD/JPY has still only travelled from 158.40 to 157.79, because oil at $78.82 hits the G10's largest energy importer through the trade account before the BoJ's wage story can help it. Keep yen exposure small and remember that a second joint MoF and US Treasury operation reverses everything in minutes. The franc is at -1 on a zero policy rate with no path off it before 2027, July CPI at 0.4% with core 0.3% and unemployment at 3.0%, but note that SNB FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July from 758.9bn and the haven complex is bid - do not press franc shorts hard in this regime. New Zealand is the anchor short at -2, with a cycle that ended after one hike, unemployment at a decade high of 5.6%, a labour cost index at 2.1% and a renewed petrol-driven inflation impulse it cannot answer. In the commodity block, gold is upgraded to a HIGH conviction long at $4,341.94 on collapsing US real-rate expectations plus a live haven bid and Chinese ETF inflows of $1.2bn in the longest streak since March; silver is upgraded from RANGE to LONG MEDIUM at $64.24 after reversing two sessions of losses, with the gold-silver ratio falling to 67.68; USOIL stays a MEDIUM long. GER40 sits at a record 26,355 after Friday's 0.7% gain - a softer Fed is a tailwind but a hawkish ECB and rising crude are not, so it stays RANGE. Everything reprices again at 12:30Z Wednesday.

USD.when: Sept 16 FOMC (the hike is being priced out)
USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. Friday's payroll report has undercut that case badly. July nonfarm payrolls CONTRACTED by 23,000 against +83,000 to +95,000 expected, the prior two months were revised down by a combined 146,000, and June was cut to +20,000. The fall in unemployment to 4.1% from 4.2% is a participation artefact - participation dropped to 61.4%, a five-year low. Average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y, the weakest since May 2021, which removes the wage-inflation channel the dissenters relied on. Rate futures now price a 43.9% chance of a September hike, down from 57% before the release, with hold probability at 60.4%. The hawkish reads still on the board are real but no longer decisive: Lisa Cook said in Anchorage she is prepared to raise rates, initial claims are at a cycle-low four-week average of 198,750, announced layoffs are the lowest in two years and unit labour costs rose just 1.3%. Trump has meanwhile said publicly that Warsh would like lower rates but is constrained by a political board. June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5%. July CPI on Aug 12 is now the deciding input.

EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, headline refi 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23. The ECB's July communication is the operative text: it warned the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to emerge, and Lagarde said the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they are to drive broader inflation through second-round effects. Euro-area energy inflation has now accelerated to 10.0% from 8.5% in July and crude is up a third straight session, so that channel is live rather than closing. The domestic leg stands on its own: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5%, services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, final composite PMI 52.0 with services 51.7 and manufacturing 51.9, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%, ZEW economic sentiment 23.4 from 9.5. The counterargument is pipeline disinflation - producer prices decelerating to 4.6% y/y from 5.9%, food inflation at 1.2%, and June retail sales falling 0.3% m/m.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. June CPI 2.6% with core 2.6% and services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wages 4.3%, unemployment 4.9% - and July PMIs were revised up again to services 52.1 and composite 52.2 from a sub-50 June. Q1 GDP was +0.6% q/q. The soft spots are the claimant count rising 6.7k and manufacturing at 51.9. A net energy importer facing a renewed crude bid with the most inflation-sensitive committee in the G10 keeps the hawkish tail alive rather than the dovish one; TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. Q2 GDP on Aug 13 is the first real domestic input in two weeks and the labour market report lands Aug 11.

JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The wage leg is intact - June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y with base pay accelerating to 3.4% from 3.0%, real earnings positive for a sixth month, and nominal growth above 3% for five straight months, the longest run in 34 years. The Bank has warned for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed target and said discussions will focus on upside price risks. June CPI rose to 1.7% from 1.5% with core at 1.6%, and Tokyo July core CPI jumped to 1.9% from 1.6%. What is not working is the tape: the dollar was sold hard on Friday's payrolls and USD/JPY has still only reached 157.79 against 158.40 on Friday morning, because crude at $78.82 hits Japan's trade account - already at a JPY 407bn deficit with terms of trade at 82.71 - before the inflation case can help the currency. Q2 GDP lands Aug 16 23:50Z. A second joint MoF and US Treasury operation remains the fastest route to a yen repricing.

AUD.note: Cash rate 4.35% after three hikes in 2026 (Feb 3.85%, Mar 4.10%, May 4.35%) on the energy shock, still the highest in the G10. Q2 headline CPI cooled to 3.8% from 4.0% and trimmed mean held 3.6%, but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% - that is not a clean pause profile, and the crude rebound removes the disinflationary Q3 assumption the dovish case rested on. Labour is solid with employment +76,343 in June, unemployment 4.4% and participation up to 67.0%. July PMIs are strong at services 53.6, composite 53.2 and manufacturing 52.0, consumer confidence improved to 83.9, and June trade swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus. TE's model still carries 4.60%. All 37 economists in the Reuters poll and all four majors expect a hold, so tomorrow is entirely about the Statement on Monetary Policy and Bullock's presser at 05:30Z - a retained willingness to hike supports AUD, any softening takes the hawkish tail out in one session. The dovish input is July consumer inflation expectations collapsing to 4.7% from 5.5%.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, and that cycle is finished. Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015; underutilisation widened to 13.8%; the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y; and employment rose 0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. The Q2 CPI of 4.1% that triggered July's move was 27.5% petrol, and with WTI back at $78.82 New Zealand faces a renewed imported inflation impulse it has no capacity to answer - a worse combination than either problem alone. The offset is domestic sentiment, which keeps improving: July ANZ business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3 from 91.3, manufacturing PMI 59.7 and composite 53.6. Two-year inflation expectations 2.53%; the RBNZ survey lands Aug 13.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, and the July labour report does not change that because the inflation side is still undershooting - June CPI 2.8% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, both BELOW target, and core at 2.1%. What did change is everything else. July employment rose 75,100, the largest gain in two years, with full-time +38,600, part-time +36,600, unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% from 6.5% and participation rising to 65.1%; core-aged women's unemployment fell 0.3pp to 5.2% and youth unemployment dropped to 12.6% from an April peak of 14.3%. Average hourly wages rose a soft 2.8% y/y to $37.17, which is why this is a growth upgrade rather than a rate one. Add WTI at $78.82 after three straight up sessions with Brent at $84.18 and the loonie now has both a labour leg and a terms-of-trade leg. Q1 GDP was flat at 0.0% q/q with monthly GDP +0.2% in June.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast. July unemployment rose to 3.0% from 2.9% with unemployed persons at 139,276, adding a growth argument to the inflation undershoot, and producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only, so the SNB is content to let the franc slide. Two things argue caution on pressing franc shorts: FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July from 758.9bn, and the domestic activity data is turning up hard - services PMI at 63.9 from 59.8, business confidence 104, and ZEW economic sentiment flipping to +10 from -25. In a session where the haven complex is bid on Hormuz and a US labour shock, the franc moves before the policy does.

catalysts.event: Iranian parliament vote on the Hormuz transit bill
catalysts.note: The draft bars US and Israeli vessels, demands compensation from hostile states and sets penalties at 20% of cargo value. Passage or a US concession moves WTI, CAD, NZD and the metals together.

catalysts.event: MoF and US Treasury joint FX intervention watch
catalysts.note: The last operation took USD/JPY to 155.20 and the yen has since given it all back to 157.79. Officials have said they will not hesitate - keep yen-cross size small.

geopolitics: The Hormuz question is unresolved and that is precisely why crude keeps rising - the market is no longer pricing a clean reopening. Iran and Oman have made real technical progress: the two sides have agreed the geographical coordinates of a proposed safe shipping route, negotiations have covered the security and sovereignty arrangements for both states, and a joint coordination centre has been proposed to manage maritime traffic and collect vessel information. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei says the draft is in its final stage and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calls an agreement very close. But the corridor and the strait are two different questions, and Iran has now separated them explicitly. IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi told state media that the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz has its own specific mechanism, has nothing to do with the Iran-Oman negotiations, and depends on the United States fully accepting Iran's conditions and refraining from interfering in the regional process. Araghchi has added that a full reopening depends on the US honouring commitments from a June memorandum of understanding that Tehran says were violated. The draft the Iranian parliament is reviewing would bar vessels linked to the US, Israel and other hostile states from transiting until Iran is compensated for war damage, with penalties proposed at 20% of a vessel's cargo value. Vice President Vance has said the US aim is to maximise the oil and gas coming out of the strait, which is not the same thing as accepting Iran's terms. The strait has been effectively closed since February and normally carries about a quarter of seaborne oil and a fifth of global LNG. Prices reflect the stalemate rather than the progress: WTI is at $78.82 after three consecutive up sessions and Brent at $84.18, up 26% year-on-year, with the US rig count unchanged at 588. The FX transmission is cleaner than it was last week because the Fed has become the dominant global input again. Rising crude plus a Fed that just lost its September hike is a combination that lifts gold and silver together - which is why the metals have recoupled after last week's decoupling, with gold at $4,341.94 and silver reversing to $64.24. CAD is the principal currency beneficiary and now has a labour leg to go with the oil leg. The euro benefits second-hand, because the ECB tied its September hike to exactly this energy channel and euro-area energy inflation has accelerated to 10.0%. NZD is the principal casualty, with a Q2 CPI that was 27.5% petrol and a central bank that has stopped. JPY is the quiet casualty, taking the trade-account hit as the G10's largest energy importer, which is why it could not rally on Friday's dollar rout. The two-sided risk is unchanged and real: the bill has not passed, the US concession has not been made, and either development would unwind the oil premium as fast as it was rebuilt. That is why USOIL stays a MEDIUM long rather than a high-conviction one.
